options.text: Swift converts all equal signs to optional bindings automatically.
options.explanation: Swift does not rewrite code; assignment simply returns no value.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between == and === in Swift?

options.text: == compares values, whereas === compares reference identity.
options.explanation: Right. == checks Equatable value equality, while === checks class instance identity.

options.text: == operates on classes, whereas === only operates on structs.
options.explanation: Structs cannot use === because structs are value types without reference identity.

options.text: == checks memory pointers, whereas === compares hash values.
options.explanation: === checks pointer addresses, whereas == checks logical equivalence.

questions.prompt: How does the closed range operator a...b define its bounds?

options.text: It includes a but excludes the upper bound b completely.
options.explanation: Excluding the upper bound b is done by the half-open range a..<b.

options.text: It excludes both a and b, keeping only values in between.
options.explanation: Swift does not have an open range operator that excludes both endpoints.

options.text: It runs from a to b and includes both endpoint values.
options.explanation: Right. The closed range a...b contains every value from a through b.

options.text: It accepts any values even if a is strictly greater than b.
options.explanation: A closed range requires a <= b; otherwise it crashes at runtime.

questions.prompt: How does the half-open range operator a..<b behave?

options.text: It includes both endpoint values a and b in the range.
options.explanation: Including both endpoints is done by the closed range a...b.

options.text: It runs from a up to but does not include the value b.
options.explanation: Right. The half-open range includes a and ends just before b.

options.text: It excludes the starting value a but includes the end value b.
options.explanation: The half-open range always includes the lower bound a.

options.text: It repeats values infinitely until an explicit break occurs.
options.explanation: Ranges in Swift are bounded collections unless one-sided.

questions.prompt: What happens when Swift evaluates the expression 5...1 at runtime?

options.text: The program counts backwards from 5 down to 1 in order.
options.explanation: Swift ranges do not count backwards automatically.

options.text: The program converts the range into an empty collection.
options.explanation: Swift does not convert reversed bounds into an empty collection.

options.text: The compiler replaces the invalid range with nil safely.
options.explanation: Ranges are non-optional structs and do not become nil.

options.text: The program crashes with a fatal runtime boundary error.
options.explanation: Right. Closed ranges require lowerBound <= upperBound; reversing them causes a fatal trap.

questions.prompt: How do standard arithmetic operators handle integer overflow in Swift?

options.text: They trap with an immediate runtime crash to prevent errors.
options.explanation: Right. Swift stops execution safely rather than allowing corrupted numbers.

options.text: They silently wrap around to negative numbers without notice.
options.explanation: Silent wrapping requires explicit overflow operators such as &+.

options.text: They convert integers to floating-point numbers automatically.
options.explanation: Swift does not perform implicit type conversions on arithmetic overflow.

options.text: They return an optional number containing nil on overflow.
options.explanation: Standard arithmetic operators return non-optional integer values.

questions.prompt: How does short-circuit evaluation work with the nil-coalescing operator ?? in Swift?

options.text: Both sides are always evaluated before choosing a value.

options.text: The right side is only evaluated if the left side is nil.

options.text: The left side is ignored whenever a default value exists.
options.explanation: The left side is checked first; the default is used only if nil.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift's assignment operator = not return a value, and what bug does this prevent? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that assignment returns Void in Swift
Identifies that it prevents accidental assignment inside if statements
Contrasts with languages like C where if (x = y) compiles silently

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, the assignment operator = returns Void instead of the assigned value. This design prevents developers from accidentally writing assignment when equality was intended inside conditions. In languages like C, writing if (x = y) assigns y to x and compiles silently. In Swift, writing if x = y produces an immediate compile error.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Basic Operators

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between value equality == and reference identity === in Swift. Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines == as testing value equality between Equatable types
Defines === as testing whether two references point to the same class instance
Mentions that === only applies to reference types like classes

questions.modelAnswer: The == operator tests value equality by checking whether two values represent equal data through Equatable conformance. In contrast, the === operator tests reference identity. It checks whether two references point to the exact same instance in memory. Because structs and enums are value types without reference identity, === only applies to class objects.

questions.prompt: Compare the closed range operator a...b and the half-open range operator a..<b. Give one use case for each. Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that closed range includes both endpoints a and b
Explains that half-open range excludes the upper bound b
Provides appropriate use cases such as zero-indexed counts for half-open ranges

questions.modelAnswer: The closed range operator a...b includes both endpoints from a up through b. It is useful for full calendar spans, like iterating through days 1...31. The half-open range operator a..<b runs from a up to but not including b. It is ideal for zero-indexed collections, such as iterating over indices from 0..<items.count.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Basic Operators

questions.prompt: How does short-circuit evaluation work in Swift's nil-coalescing operator ??, and why is this useful? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that the right-hand operand is only evaluated when the left-hand optional is nil
Explains that if the left operand has a value, the right expression is skipped
Mentions the performance benefit of avoiding unnecessary computation or side effects

questions.modelAnswer: The nil-coalescing operator ?? uses short-circuit evaluation. If the left-hand optional contains a value, Swift unwraps that value and never evaluates the right-hand expression. The right-hand side executes only if the optional evaluates to nil. This avoids expensive computations, network calls, or unwanted side effects when a valid value already exists.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Basic Operators

questions.prompt: What happens when an arithmetic operation overflows an integer type in Swift? How does Swift differ from C in this behavior? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift traps with an immediate runtime crash on integer overflow
Contrasts with C which silently wraps or exhibits undefined behavior
Mentions that explicit overflow operators like &+ are required for wrapping in Swift

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, standard arithmetic operators check for overflow by default and cause a runtime crash if a calculation exceeds integer bounds. In contrast, C allows silent integer wraparound or undefined behavior, which often introduces security vulnerabilities. If a developer explicitly requires overflow wraparound in Swift, they must choose dedicated overflow operators like &+ or &*.
